module

public import FormalConjecturesUtil

/-!
# Erdős Problem 401

*References:*
- [erdosproblems.com/401](https://www.erdosproblems.com/401)
- [ErGr80] Erdős, P. and Graham, R., *Old and new problems and results in combinatorial number
  theory*. Monographies de L'Enseignement Mathematique (1980).
-/

@[expose] public section

open Filter

namespace Erdos401

/--
Is there some function $f(r)$ such that $f(r)\to \infty$ as $r\to\infty$, such that, for
infinitely many $n$, there exist $a_1,a_2$ with
$$a_1+a_2> n+f(r)\log n$$
such that $a_1!a_2! \mid n!2^n3^n\cdots p_r^n$?

It is ambiguous in [ErGr80] what the intended quantifiers are on the variables (they write 'is
it true that we can find $a_1+a_2>n+f(r)\log n$...'). Comparing to previous problems such as
[728] and [729] it seems most likely that they intended to ask the formulation in the problem
statement.

The answer is yes: Barreto and Leeham have used ChatGPT to provide a proof of the stated problem
(in fact essentially the same construction as their solution to [729]).
-/
@[category research solved, AMS 11, formal_proof using lean4 at "https://github.com/plby/lean-proofs/blob/1d7b3f00780b85ed0462e79a1cd5650ee9055655/src/v4.29.1/ErdosProblems/Erdos401.lean"]
theorem erdos_401 : answer(True) ↔
    ∃ f : ℕ → ℝ, Tendsto f atTop atTop ∧
      ∀ (r : ℕ) (hr : 1 ≤ r),
        {n : ℕ | ∃ a₁ a₂ : ℕ, 0 < a₁ ∧ 0 < a₂ ∧
          (a₁ : ℝ) + a₂ > n + f r * Real.log n ∧
          a₁.factorial * a₂.factorial ∣
            n.factorial * (∏ i ∈ Finset.range r, Nat.nth Nat.Prime i) ^ n}.Infinite := by
  sorry

end Erdos401

reformulations.difference: The Lean requires 0 < a₁ ∧ 0 < a₂, while the source only says "there exist a₁, a₂".
reformulations.equivalence_argument: 0! = 1! = 1, so a witness with a₁ = 0 (or a₂ = 0) can be replaced by 1 (max a 1). The divisibility a₁!a₂! ∣ n!·(p_1⋯p_r)^n is unchanged and a₁ + a₂ only grows, so the strict inequality still holds. The good sets with and without positivity are therefore equal for every f and r. The converse direction is trivial.

reformulations.difference: The source leaves the quantifier on r implicit (f(r) → ∞, a condition "for r"), and one could read it as "for all sufficiently large r". The Lean quantifies over every r ≥ 1.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: If the condition holds for all r ≥ R with some f → ∞, set g(r) = 0 for r < R and g = f otherwise. g is eventually equal to f, so g → ∞. For r < R, g(r) ≤ 0 and every n ≥ 1 is good via (a₁, a₂) = (n, 1): n + 1 > n + g(r)·log n, and n!·1! ∣ n!·P^n. So the set is infinite. The converse direction is immediate.

review.notes:
No misformalization found. The Lean states the problem exactly as erdosproblems.com/401 now poses it: there is f : ℕ → ℝ with f → ∞ such that for every r ≥ 1 there are infinitely many n with positive a₁, a₂, a₁ + a₂ > n + f(r) log n, and a₁!a₂! ∣ n!·(p_1⋯p_r)^n. The product ∏_{i<r} Nat.nth Nat.Prime i is p_1⋯p_r; I checked r = 2 and r = 3 in Lean.

The original book (Erdős–Graham 1980, p.78) is ambiguous about the quantifier on n: "is it true that we can find a₁+a₂>n+d_r log n with d_r→∞ as r→∞ so that n!2^n3^n⋯p_r^n/(a₁!a₂!) is an integer?" The site chose the per-r "infinitely many n" reading, and the Lean follows it. In the forum Bloom calls the earlier 'for all large n' wording his misreading, and Sothanaphan disproved that version.

The statement is not degenerate: (n, 1) only helps when f(r) ≤ 0, and for q = p_{r+1} Legendre's formula gives a₁ + a₂ ≤ n + O(q log n / log q). This is the same scale as the proved ω(r) ~ (q−1)/log q.

Status and proof link:
- `research solved` with `answer(True)` matches the source (PROVED (LEAN)).
- The formal_proof link is a stable commit link to a sorry-free file whose theorem_1 is the per-r statement for an explicit ω(r) = (9/1120)(q−1)/log q with q = p_{r+1}.
- That file does not prove Tendsto ω atTop atTop. I proved it in a few lines, and with it theorem_1 implies the repository's right-hand side (checked in Lean with theorem_1 as a hypothesis).
- I could not build the pinned Lean 4.29.1 file in the sandbox. The author's 4.33.0 port has an identical main statement and identical definitions of p, P, γ and ω. It compiles against the sandbox Mathlib 4.33.1 with exit code 0, no errors, and axioms [propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound].
